p.src: After Xu Ning had finished selecting the troops, he descended from the Hall of Righteousness, took up a hooked lance, and demonstrated a complete sequence himself. Everyone cheered at the sight. Xu Ning then instructed the soldiers: “Whenever this weapon is used on horseback, its footwork begins at the waist and hips. Its seven upper and middle lines comprise three hooks, four parries, one thrust, and one separation, making nine transformations in all. When wielded on foot, the hooked lance is likewise exceptionally effective. Begin with eight steps and four parries to sweep open the opponent’s guard; at twelve steps make one transformation, and at sixteen steps execute a great turn. Separate, hook, reap, thrust, and strike; over twenty-four steps, shift upward and close downward, hooking east and parrying west; at thirty-six steps, shield the whole body and overcome the hard and the strong. This is the orthodox method of the hooked lance. A mnemonic verse bears witness: Four parries and three hooks command seven lines; divided into nine transformations, they accord with wondrous strategy. Twenty-four steps shift forward and back; sixteen reversals make the great encircling turn.” Xu Ning demonstrated each sequence of the orthodox method for the chieftains to see. When the soldiers saw Xu Ning wield the hooked lance, they were all delighted. Beginning that very day, the chosen elite men of strength trained day and night. He also taught the infantry to conceal themselves in woods and lie hidden in grass, using the three secret low-line methods of hooking hooves and dragging legs. In less than half a month, he had trained five to seven hundred men of the stronghold. Song Jiang and the chieftains were overjoyed when they inspected them and made ready to break the enemy.

p.src: As for Huyan Zhuo, ever since losing Peng Qi and Ling Zhen, he brought his cavalry to the water’s edge each day to challenge the outlaws to battle. The stronghold merely ordered its naval chieftains to guard every beachhead securely, while hidden stakes were driven beneath the water. Though Huyan Zhuo sent scouts along the routes north and west of the mountain, he could by no means approach the stronghold itself. At Liangshan Marsh, meanwhile, Ling Zhen was ordered to manufacture all manner of cannon, and a fixed day and hour were set for descending the mountain to meet the enemy. The soldiers learning to wield the hooked lance had all mastered it. Song Jiang said, “In my poor and shallow judgment, I have conceived a plan, though I do not know whether it will accord with everyone’s wishes.” Wu Yong said, “We should like to hear its outline.” Song Jiang said, “Tomorrow we shall use not a single cavalryman; all the chieftains will fight on foot. The military methods of Sun and Wu are especially advantageous amid wooded mountains and marshy ground. We shall send the infantry down the mountain, divide them into ten companies, and have them lure the enemy. Whenever the enemy cavalry comes charging down upon them, they are all to flee pell-mell into the reeds, brambles, and woods. We shall first conceal the hooked-lance troops there, placing ten grappling-hook men among every ten skilled hooked-lance soldiers. As soon as the horses arrive, they will hook and overturn them in one sweep; then the grappling hooks will catch the riders and drag them in to be seized. We shall lay the same ambushes on level ground and narrow roads. What do you think of this method?” Scholar Wu said, “That is precisely how we should conceal our troops and capture their generals.” Xu Ning said, “Hooked lances together with grappling hooks are exactly suited to this method.”

p.src: Now the tale divides in two. Let us first tell how Song Jiang sounded the gong to recall his troops to the mountain, where rewards were given according to merit. Of the three thousand linked armoured horses, half had been brought down by the hooked sickle-spears and had injured their hooves. Their leather armour was stripped off, and they were used for meat and fodder; the other two-thirds, being fine horses, were led up the mountain, fed, and kept as mounts. All the armoured soldiers were captured alive and taken up the mountain. The five thousand infantrymen were tightly surrounded on three sides. Those who fled toward the central army for shelter were all dragged down and captured with hooked sickle-spears; those who fled for their lives toward the water were surrounded by the naval commanders, herded aboard boats, hauled across to the shore, arrested, and taken up the mountain. All the horses and soldiers previously seized by the enemy were recaptured and brought back to the stronghold. They dismantled Huyan Zhuo’s entire stockade and brought the materials to the waterside harbour, where they built a small outpost. They also constructed two more lookout inns and other buildings, and once again assigned Sun Xin, Madam Gu, Shi Yong, and Shi Qian to operate the two establishments. Liu Tang and Du Qian captured Han Tao, bound him, and escorted him to the mountain stronghold. When Song Jiang saw him, he personally untied his bonds, invited him into the hall, and spoke courteously with him over a banquet. He had Peng Qi and Ling Zhen urge Han Tao to join the band. Han Tao, too, was numbered among the Seventy-Two Earthly Fiends; their temperaments naturally accorded, and he became a chieftain of Liangshan Marsh. Song Jiang then had a letter written and sent men to Chen Prefecture to bring Han Tao’s family to the stronghold, so that they might be reunited. Song Jiang rejoiced at having broken the linked cavalry and acquired so many soldiers, horses, suits of armour, helmets, and blades. Every day he held banquets in celebration. He reassigned the guards along every route as before and kept watch against government troops. Of this no more need be said.

p.src: After two days on the road, he was both hungry and thirsty that evening. Seeing a village tavern by the roadside, Huyan Zhuo dismounted and tethered his horse to a tree before the door. He entered the tavern, laid his whips on the table, sat down, and called for the keeper to bring him wine and meat. The keeper said, “This humble establishment sells only wine. If you want meat, a sheep has just been slaughtered in the village. If you wish, I can go and buy some.” Huyan Zhuo untied the provision pouch at his waist, took out some fragments of silver exchanged from his gold belt, and handed them to the keeper, saying, “Buy me a leg of mutton and cook it, and also see to fodder for my horse. I shall lodge here for tonight and make my way to Qingzhou Prefecture tomorrow.” The keeper said, “You may certainly stay here, sir, but we have no decent bed or curtains.” Huyan Zhuo said, “I am a soldier in the field. Any place to rest will do.” Taking the silver, the keeper went off to buy the mutton. Huyan Zhuo removed the clothes and armor strapped to his horse’s back, loosened its girth, and sat before the door. After waiting quite a while, he saw the keeper return carrying a leg of mutton. Huyan Zhuo told him to cook it, buy three jin of flour to make flatbread, and bring two horns of wine. While cooking the meat and making the bread, the keeper heated water for Huyan Zhuo to wash his feet, then led the horse to a small shed behind the house. As the keeper chopped hay and cooked the feed, Huyan Zhuo first called for hot wine and drank for a while. Before long the meat was done. Huyan Zhuo called the keeper over and gave him some wine and meat too, instructing him, “I am an officer of the imperial army. Leading their lesser bandits away, they crossed a nearby ridge and made camp.

p.src: Meanwhile, Huyan Zhuo sat brooding in his tent. “I expected to sweep through this place like a knife splitting bamboo and capture these brigands at once. Who could have known I would meet such opponents again! How cruelly fortune treats me!” Just as he found himself at a loss, a messenger came from Prefect Murong with this summons: “The prefect orders the general to bring his troops back for the defense of the city. The outlaws Kong Ming and Kong Liang of White Tiger Mountain have brought men to Qingzhou to seize provisions. Fearing for the government storehouses, he has specially sent me to request that the general return and guard the city.” On hearing this, Huyan Zhuo seized the opportunity and led his forces back to Qingzhou that very night.

Li Zhong and Zhou Tong led their men down from the mountain and respectfully invited the three chiefs up to the stronghold. There they slaughtered oxen and horses and entertained them with a feast, while sending men down the mountain to learn what had happened farther along the road.

p.src: Now Huyan Zhuo, leading his army back beneath the city walls, saw a body of troops approaching the city. At their head were the sons of Squire Kong, who lived below White Tiger Mountain: Kong Ming, the Hairy-Headed Star, and Kong Liang, the Lone Fiery Star. The brothers had quarreled with a wealthy man of their district and killed his entire household, high and low. They then gathered five to seven hundred followers, occupied White Tiger Mountain, and took to plundering homes and travelers. Their uncle Kong Bin had been arrested in Qingzhou by Prefect Murong and imprisoned. Kong Ming and Kong Liang had therefore mustered the men of their stronghold and come expressly to attack Qingzhou and rescue their uncle Kong Bin; but they ran straight into Huyan Zhuo's army. The two forces surged together and began fighting, and Huyan Zhuo rode out before the battle line. Watching from the city tower, Prefect Murong saw Kong Ming spur out first with his spear leveled, charging straight at Huyan Zhuo. Their horses met, and they fought for more than twenty bouts. Huyan Zhuo wished to display his prowess before the prefect, while Kong Ming was an indifferent fighter who could do no more than parry and fend off the blows. As the struggle grew fierce, Huyan Zhuo seized Kong Ming alive from the saddle, and Kong Liang had no choice but to lead the lesser bandits in flight. From the defensive tower Prefect Murong pointed after them and ordered Huyan Zhuo to give chase. The government troops swept forward and captured more than a hundred men alive. Kong Liang suffered a crushing defeat, and his men scattered in every direction. At nightfall he found an old temple where he could rest.

p.src: Meanwhile, Huyan Zhuo brought the captive Kong Ming into the city and presented himself before Prefect Murong. The prefect was delighted. He ordered Kong Ming fastened in a heavy cangue and cast into prison, to be confined together with Kong Bin. He rewarded the troops and entertained Huyan Zhuo, questioning him closely about events at Peach Blossom Mountain. Huyan Zhuo said, “I expected it to be like catching a turtle in a jar—the moment I reached out, they would be mine. But for no reason at all, another band of outlaws came to their aid. Among them were a monk and a blue-faced giant. I fought each of them in turn, but neither contest was decided. Their martial skill is far from ordinary and not of the sort found among common outlaws. That is why I failed to capture them.” Prefect Murong said, “That monk was once Lu Da, a major serving under the Senior Military Commissioner of Yan'an Prefecture. He has now shaved his head and become a monk, and is called Lu Zhishen, the Flowery Monk. The blue-faced giant was likewise once a military commissioner in the Palace Commandant's Office in the Eastern Capital. He is called Yang Zhi, the Blue-Faced Beast. There is also a pilgrim named Wu Song, formerly the constable who slew the tiger on Jingyang Ridge. These three occupy Twin Dragons Mountain, plundering homes and travelers. Time and again they have resisted government troops and killed several officers charged with pursuing bandits. To this day they have never been captured.” Huyan Zhuo said, “I could see that those fellows were consummate fighters. So they were Commissioner Yang and Major Lu! Their fame is well deserved. Set your mind at ease, Excellency. I have now seen what they can do. Sooner or later, I shall capture every one of them alive and deliver them to the authorities.” The prefect was overjoyed. When the banquet was over, he invited Huyan Zhuo to rest in the guest quarters; but no more of this.

p.src: Seeing that it was Wu Song, Kong Liang hurriedly tumbled from his saddle, bowed, and said, “Have you been well, good sir?” Wu Song promptly returned his greeting, helped him up, and asked, “I heard that you brothers had occupied White Tiger Mountain and gathered a band of righteous men. What has brought you here today?” Kong Liang recounted how they had tried to rescue their uncle Kong Bin, only for his elder brother to be captured. Wu Song said, “Do not be alarmed. p.src: Kong Liang bowed and thanked Wu Song. After they had waited for some time, Lu Zhishen and Yang Zhi appeared, riding side by side. Wu Song presented Kong Liang to the two chiefs and explained in detail: “When Song Jiang and I once met at his manor, we imposed greatly upon his hospitality. Today we should put brotherhood first. Let us unite the forces of all three mountains, attack Qingzhou, kill Prefect Murong, capture Huyan Zhuo, and seize the money and provisions in the government storehouses for the use of our strongholds. What do you say?” Lu Zhishen said, “I was thinking the very same thing. Send someone at once to Peach Blossom Mountain to inform Li Zhong and Zhou Tong and tell them to bring their lads. Then the forces of our three mountains will attack Qingzhou together.”

I do not say this to diminish our own courage, but if we mean to attack Qingzhou, only by following one proposal of mine can we take it within a matter of days.” Wu Song said, “Brother, we should like to hear your plan.” Yang Zhi then spoke at great length, saying more than could be told in a single sitting.
